rationale: Prov.9.1 opens third-person narration whose subject is personified Wisdom (חכמות, oshb:Prov.9.1), building her house and hewing her seven pillars; the same figure prepares the meal in 9:2 and sends her maidens to call out in 9:3, and their call becomes her own quoted summons in 9:4-6, closing on “Walk in the way of understanding.” (web:Prov.9.6) That imperative answers the invitation the scene opened with. Prov.9.7 changes both subject and mode, dropping the personified figure for anonymous participial sayings about correcting a mocker, so the span is held to 9:6.
rejected_alternative: Extending the span through 9:9 to align with the petuchah recorded there was rejected: the mark falls after a discourse break that has already occurred at 9:7, so it corroborates the following unit's close, not this one's.

the petuchah at Prov.8.36 (single-witness) sits at the front seam, immediately before this span opens
device_notes: Narrative-to-direct-speech progression (third-person build/prepare/send, then Wisdom's own first-person invitation); synthetic, not antithetic — no wicked/righteous contrast pair occurs in this span.

rationale: This span pivots from the banquet scene to a short run built on second-person imperatives: 9:8’s “Don’t reprove a scoffer... Reprove a wise person” and 9:9’s “Instruct a wise person... Teach a righteous person” (web:Prov.9.8, web:Prov.9.9) bracket the participial maxim of 9:7 about a corrector's reward. The imperative core (אל תוכח, oshb:Prov.9.8, skeleton tier; תן, הודע, oshb:Prov.9.9, skeleton tier) marks a different mood from the declarative maxims that follow at 9:10, where the verbs turn conditional and nominal.
rejected_alternative: Treating 9:7-9:12 as one combined unit was rejected: 9:8-9:9 carry second-person imperatives addressed to a hearer, while 9:10-9:12 shift to nominal and conditional maxims without an imperative verb, a mood boundary the petuchah at 9:9 corroborates.

petuchah at Prov.9.9 (single-witness) falls at this span's own closing verse
device_notes: Participle-imperative-imperative sequence; the mocker/wise-person contrast is synonymous rather than antithetic (no adversative clause structure), a texture distinct from the antithetic bicola that dominate the following collection.

rationale: 9:10's nominal thesis — the fear of Yahweh as wisdom's beginning — opens a short run without an imperative verb, continuing in 9:11 with a first-person clause, “For by me your days will be multiplied” (web:Prov.9.11), that returns to Wisdom's own voice from 9:1-6, and closing in 9:12's conditional maxim about bearing one's own wisdom or mockery. Prov.9.13 then introduces a different subject, a foolish woman, ending this run before that shift.
rejected_alternative: Folding 9:10-9:12 into the following Woman Folly scene was rejected: 9:13 introduces a new grammatical subject that 9:10-9:12's fear-of-Yahweh and self-benefit maxims do not carry.

device_notes: Nominal thesis followed by first-person and conditional clauses; the adversative "but"-clause typical of the surrounding admonition unit and the following sentence collection drops out of this span.

rationale: 9:13 introduces a new subject, the foolish woman (אשת כסילות, oshb:Prov.9.13), and the same figure carries the action through her seating at the city gate in 9:14, her call to passersby in 9:15, and her quoted invitation in 9:16-17, closing in 9:18 on the narrator's verdict that her guests are in Sheol's depths. The invitation formula of 9:16, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here” (web:Prov.9.16), repeats the bare consonants מי פתי יסר הנה (oshb:Prov.9.16) already spoken by Wisdom at Prov.9.4, marking this span as the deliberate counter-scene to 9:1-6 rather than a continuation of the intervening sayings of 9:7-9:12.
rejected_alternative: Splitting off 9:17 as a standalone saying was rejected: it continues Folly's own direct speech opened in 9:16, keeping the same subject and addressee.

rationale: 10:16 and 10:17 both build on the exact prefixed phrase לחיים ("to life", oshb:Prov.10.16, oshb:Prov.10.17); a skeleton sweep of that precise spelling returns only 4 verses in the whole book, and these two are the only adjacent pair among them (the others are Prov.11.19 and Prov.19.23). Both verses build the same "way/fruit that leads to life" argument: 10:16 names the righteous person's labor as leading to life, 10:17 names the path of life itself as the one who heeds correction, and the pairing forms a short envelope on the reward of a disciplined life before 10:18 turns to the topic of hidden hatred and slander.
rejected_alternative: Reading 10:16 and 10:17 as unrelated separate proverbs was set aside given the rarity of their shared exact phrase לחיים (oshb:Prov.10.16); treating the cluster as reaching into 10:15 or 10:18 was also rejected, since neither of those verses carries that phrase or its life/way argument.

device_notes: Both cola are synthetic in frame (10:16 opposes life/sin as parallel outcomes rather than contrasting subjects; 10:17 opposes the one who heeds correction with the one who forsakes it inside one shared life/straying frame). rationale: 10:32 ends on the noun תהפכות ("perversities/perverse", oshb:Prov.10.32); in 10:31 the same noun sits construct-medial, the sixth of seven words (ולשון תהפכות, "and a tongue of perverse things"), governed by the verse's own closing verb תִּכָּרֵֽת ("will be cut off") rather than closing the verse itself (oshb:Prov.10.31). A skeleton sweep of the noun תהפכות returns 9 verses book-wide, and this adjacent pair is where two of those hits happen to stand next to each other. Both verses also open with a construct chain naming a speech organ of the righteous — פי צדיק ("mouth of the righteous") in 10:31, שפתי צדיק ("lips of the righteous") in 10:32 — closing the chapter's run of righteous/wicked speech sayings on a paired formulation.
rejected_alternative: Reading 10:31 and 10:32 as separate proverbs was set aside given the rarity of their shared closing noun; extending the cluster back into 10:30 was also rejected, since that verse's land-tenure topic shares neither the noun nor the speech-organ construct chain.

rationale: 11:5 and 11:6 both open with the same construct noun צדקת ("righteousness of", oshb:Prov.11.5, oshb:Prov.11.6); a skeleton sweep of that exact construct spelling returns 2 verses in the whole book. Both then name a virtue-bearer (the blameless in 11:5, the upright in 11:6) and close on a vav-clause in which the wicked or treacherous fall or are trapped by their own vice, but the two verses do not share person or number: 11:5 runs singular throughout (a bare verb with a 3ms-suffixed object, then a 3ms parallel verb), while 11:6 runs plural (a verb carrying a 3mp object suffix, then a 3mp parallel verb). The shared ground is the exclusive צדקת construct-opener plus the vice-triggered-downfall template, not a uniform person or number — a paired two-line run that ends before 11:7 changes both subject and construction.
rejected_alternative: Extending the cluster to include 11:4 or 11:7 was rejected: neither carries the צדקת-opening (oshb:Prov.11.5) construct chain or the virtue-guides/vice-destroys template shared by 11:5 and 11:6 alone.

rationale: 11:8 and 11:9 share the book's only two occurrences of the root חלץ (oshb:Prov.11.8, oshb:Prov.11.9; "draw out, deliver"): the final-form spelling חלץ in נֶחֱלָ֑ץ (Niphal, oshb:Prov.11.8, 1 verse) and the medial-form spelling חלצ in יֵחָלֵֽצוּ (Niphal, oshb:Prov.11.9, 1 verse) — combined 2 of 915 verses book-wide (skeleton tier, verse-count unit). Both occurrences are Niphal (passive) forms; WEB's own translation renders both passively (“is delivered”, web:Prov.11.8; “will be delivered”, web:Prov.11.9); both sit clause-final in their own colon; both are predicated of the righteous, singular צדיק (oshb:Prov.11.8) at 11:8 and plural צדיקים (oshb:Prov.11.9) at 11:9 (skeleton). 11:8 pictures the righteous delivered from trouble as the wicked takes his place (a substitution image); 11:9 pictures the righteous delivered through knowledge, set against a neighbor destroyed by the godless man's mouth (a mouth/knowledge image). The two verses run the shared deliverance verb across two different scenario pictures, closing this stretch before 11:10 turns to the city's own reaction to each party's fortune.
rejected_alternative: Reading 11:8 and 11:9 as two unrelated single proverbs was rejected: the root חלץ (oshb:Prov.11.8, oshb:Prov.11.9) occurs nowhere else in the book (1+1=2 of 915 verses, skeleton tier, allography-aware), an exclusivity too narrow to dismiss as chapter-generic vocabulary; the deliverance verb's shared clause-final placement and righteous-party subject across both verses outweighs the verses' distinct scenario imagery (substitution at 11:8, mouth/knowledge at 11:9), which is retained as intra-cluster texture rather than a dividing feature.

rationale: 11:25 and 11:26 both carry the noun ברכה ("blessing", oshb:Prov.11.25, skeleton tier; oshb:Prov.11.26, skeleton tier): 11:25 calls the generous person a נפש ברכה ("soul of blessing") who will be made fat, and 11:26 promises ברכה ("blessing") on the head of one who sells rather than withholds grain — both verses argue the same behavior pattern (giving/selling versus withholding) and its reward under that one shared noun.
